overview: This unit covers the modular RISC-V instruction set architecture (RISC-V-ISA), registers and their usage conventions (Verwendungskonventionen), and signed and unsigned arithmetic (signed- und unsigned-Arithmetik). It explains how multiplication (Multiplikation), division (Division), and shifts (Shifts) change bit patterns, when shifts are equivalent to multiplication or division, and how pseudoinstructions (Pseudobefehle) and immediate instructions (Immediate-Befehle) are used. Step-by-step checks of register values, signs, register allocation, and loop execution help prevent errors in assembly programs.

entries.term: RISC-V base and extensions (RISC-V-Basis und Erweiterungen)
entries.short: RISC-V is an open, modular instruction set whose base can be supplemented with optional extensions.
entries.explanation: `RV32` denotes a 32-bit variant; the number indicates the register width in bits. `I` stands for the integer base, with about 40 base instructions, and `M` adds multiplication and division instructions. Other extensions include `F` for floating-point, `A` for atomic operations, and `V` for vector operations. `RV32I` denotes the 32-bit base; `RV32IM` adds the M extension.
entries.example: A processor with `RV32IM` can use base instructions from `RV32I` and M instructions such as `mul` and `div`.
pitfalls: `RV32` specifies the register width; `I` and `M` identify components of the instruction set.
The available instructions depend on the base and the implemented extensions.
entries.heading: RISC-V: Basis und Erweiterungen

entries.short: RV32I has 32 registers, from `x0` to `x31`, each 32 bits wide.
entries.explanation: Registers reside in the processor and serve as sources and destinations for instruction operands. `x0` always supplies the value zero and cannot be changed. No particular initial value may be assumed for any other register. A program must therefore set or load any values it needs before using them.
entries.example: In `add t0, t1, t2`, values are read from two registers and the result is written to a register.
pitfalls: Registers other than `x0` are not automatically zero.
related: Zero register x0 and initial values
entries.heading: Register

entries.short: Names such as `a0`, `s0`, and `t0` are conventional aliases for registers `x0` through `x31`.
entries.explanation: The aliases describe customary roles, not different register types. `x0` is called `zero`, `x1` is `ra`, `x2` is `sp`, `x3` is `gp`, and `x4` is `tp`. `x5` through `x7` are called `t0` through `t2`, `x8` is `s0` or `fp`, `x9` is `s1`, `x10` through `x17` are `a0` through `a7`, `x18` through `x27` are `s2` through `s11`, and `x28` through `x31` are `t3` through `t6`. `a0` and `a1` are also commonly used for return values; the specific calling convention defines how registers are used in subroutine calls.
entries.example: `a0` and `x10` refer to the same register; `a0` highlights its customary role as an argument or return-value register.
pitfalls: An alias does not change the register's width or hardware properties.
The register name alone does not guarantee that it contains a particular value.
related: Zero register x0 and initial values
entries.heading: Register

entries.term: Zero register x0 and initial values (Nullregister x0 und Anfangswerte)
entries.short: `x0` always supplies zero, while no initial value may be assumed for other registers.
entries.explanation: Register `x0` is hardwired to zero; an attempt to write to it does not change its value. All other registers can contain arbitrary values at the start of a program section unless the code sets them beforehand. A program must therefore explicitly load or compute any values it needs.
entries.example: `addi t0, x0, 7` sets `t0` to 7 because `x0` supplies zero as the source.
pitfalls: Do not assume that a register such as `t0` initially contains zero.
`x0` is not an ordinary register whose value can be changed by a write instruction.
entries.heading: Register

entries.term: Signed and unsigned interpretation in M instructions (Signed- und Unsigned-Interpretation bei M-Befehlen)
entries.short: The same bit pattern can represent different numbers when interpreted as signed or unsigned, so M instructions provide different interpretations.
entries.explanation: Under a signed interpretation, a bit pattern is read as a two's-complement signed number; under an unsigned interpretation, it is read as a nonnegative number. The bits themselves do not change, but the numerical value and the result of a multiplication or division can differ. The respective M instructions specify which interpretation applies to the operation.
entries.example: The 4-bit pattern `1101` represents 13 as unsigned and −3 as signed in two's complement.
pitfalls: The bits alone do not determine a signed or unsigned value; the interpretation must be known.
related: Multiplication instructions mul, mulh, mulhu, and mulhsu
Division and remainder instructions div, divu, rem, and remu
entries.heading: Multiplikation und Division: signed oder unsigned?

entries.term: Multiplication instructions mul, mulh, mulhu, and mulhsu (Multiplikationsbefehle mul, mulh, mulhu und mulhsu)
entries.short: `mul` returns the lower product bits, while `mulh`, `mulhu`, and `mulhsu` return the upper bits according to the signedness interpretation.
entries.explanation: Two 32-bit operands can produce a product of up to 64 bits. `mul` writes the lower 32 product bits; for the same bit patterns, these are independent of whether the operands are interpreted as signed or unsigned. `mulh` returns the upper 32 bits for two signed operands, `mulhu` for two unsigned operands, and `mulhsu` for a signed first operand and an unsigned second operand. To obtain the full 64-bit product, combine the lower bits from `mul` with the appropriately computed upper part.
entries.example: With four bits per operand, `1101 · 0010` yields `0001 1010` (26) as unsigned and `1111 1010` (−6) as signed; in both cases, the lower four bits are `1010`.
pitfalls: `mul` does not automatically return the full 64-bit product.
For the upper product bits, the signed or unsigned interpretation of both operands must match the intended calculation.
related: Signed and unsigned interpretation in M instructions
entries.heading: Multiplikation und Division: signed oder unsigned?

entries.term: Division and remainder instructions div, divu, rem, and remu (Divisions- und Restbefehle div, divu, rem und remu)
entries.short: `div` and `rem` operate on signed values, while `divu` and `remu` compute an unsigned quotient and remainder, respectively.
entries.explanation: `div` computes a signed quotient, and `rem` computes the corresponding signed remainder. `divu` and `remu` perform the corresponding operations on operands interpreted as unsigned. Signed integer division rounds toward zero; for negative odd numbers, its result can therefore differ from an arithmetic right shift.
entries.example: For signed `−47`, `div` by 2 yields `−23`; an arithmetic right shift by one position yields `−24`.
pitfalls: `div` and `divu` are not interchangeable when a bit pattern is intended to represent a signed negative number.
For negative odd numbers, a right shift is not always equivalent to signed division by 2.
related: Signed and unsigned interpretation in M instructions
entries.heading: Multiplikation und Division: signed oder unsigned?

entries.term: Shift instructions and shift amount (Shift-Befehle und Shiftweite)
entries.short: RISC-V instructions specify the shift direction and fill rule, while the suffix `i` indicates an immediate shift amount.
entries.explanation: For `sll`, `srl`, and `sra`, the shift amount comes from a register; for `slli`, `srli`, and `srai`, it is given as an immediate in the instruction. The instruction family also determines the shift direction and how the vacated bit positions are filled. In RISC-V, `srl` and `sra` clearly distinguish the two kinds of right shift. Symbols such as `>>` or `>>>` can have different meanings in different programming languages.
entries.example: `slli t1, t0, 1` shifts the value in `t0` one position to the left and writes the result to `t1`.
pitfalls: The `i` in `slli` indicates an immediate for the shift amount; it does not mean “arithmetic.”
Do not infer a specific RISC-V shift type from `>>` alone.
related: Logical right shift (Logischer Rechtsshift; srl, srli)
Arithmetic right shift (Arithmetischer Rechtsshift; sra, srai)
entries.heading: Shifts: Bits verschieben

entries.short: `sll` and `slli` shift bits to the left, fill with zeros on the right, and discard high bits shifted out.
entries.explanation: A left shift by one position moves each bit pattern one position to the left. The result can be interpreted as multiplication by 2 without information loss only if the mathematical product is representable at the chosen word width. The bit operation is the same for signed and unsigned interpretations. In the event of overflow, only the result at the register width is retained.
entries.example: With 8 bits, `0010 1100` (44) becomes `0101 1000` (88). The pattern `1101 0000` becomes `1010 0000`; as unsigned values, this corresponds to 208 becoming 160 after the shifted-out bit is discarded.
pitfalls: A left shift can lose significant high bits.
Equality with mathematical multiplication holds only if the result fits in the width being considered.
entries.heading: Links um eine Stelle: Multiplikation mit 2

entries.term: Logical right shift (Logischer Rechtsshift; srl, srli)
entries.short: `srl` and `srli` shift bits to the right and fill the vacated high bits with zeros.
entries.explanation: In a logical right shift, the remaining bits move to the right and bits at the right edge are discarded. Zeros are inserted on the left regardless of the previous sign. This operation is especially useful when a bit pattern is treated as an unsigned number or a bit field is shifted.
entries.example: The 8-bit pattern `1101 0000` becomes `0110 1000` after a logical shift right by one position; as unsigned values, this corresponds to 208 divided by 2, which equals 104.
pitfalls: For a bit pattern interpreted as negative, the sign bit is not preserved.
A logical right shift is not the same as an arithmetic right shift.
entries.heading: Rechts um eine Stelle: zwei Arten

entries.term: Arithmetic right shift (Arithmetischer Rechtsshift; sra, srai)
entries.short: `sra` and `srai` shift bits to the right and fill on the left with copies of the sign bit.
entries.explanation: Copying the most significant bit preserves the sign of a two's-complement result. For even numbers, an arithmetic right shift by one position is equivalent to division by 2. For negative odd numbers, however, the shift rounds toward the smaller value, while signed integer division rounds toward zero. Therefore, use `div` for true signed division.
pitfalls: Filling with the sign bit distinguishes `sra` from `srl`.
For negative odd values, `srai` does not replace signed division.
related: Division and remainder instructions div, divu, rem, and remu
entries.heading: Rechts um eine Stelle: zwei Arten

entries.short: A pseudoinstruction is a readable assembly form that the assembler translates into one or more actual machine instructions.
entries.explanation: Pseudoinstructions make assembly programs shorter and easier to read, but they are not machine instructions of their own. One possible expansion for `mv t0, t1` is `addi t0, t1, 0`; `not t0, t1` can be implemented as `xori t0, t1, -1`. `neg t0, t1` can, for example, be expressed as `sub t0, x0, t1`. The expansion depends on the pseudoinstruction and, in some cases, on the constant.
entries.example: `mv t0, t1` copies the value from `t1` to `t0`; one possible RV32I expansion is `addi t0, t1, 0`.
pitfalls: A pseudoinstruction is not necessarily exactly one machine instruction.
The specific expansion can depend on the constant used.
entries.heading: Pseudobefehle

entries.short: `li` loads a constant into a register, with the assembler generating a suitable instruction sequence depending on the constant.
entries.explanation: For a small constant such as 7, `li t0, 7` can, for example, become `addi t0, x0, 7`. Larger constants do not necessarily fit in a single immediate and may require several actual instructions, such as `lui` and `addi`. Thus, `li` has no single fixed expansion.
entries.example: One possible expansion of `li t0, 7` is `addi t0, x0, 7`.
pitfalls: Do not assume that every `li` generates exactly one machine instruction.
For larger constants, the assembler may need to split the constant into parts.
entries.heading: Pseudobefehle

entries.short: An immediate is a constant encoded directly in a machine instruction.
entries.explanation: An instruction with an immediate gets an operand value from the instruction itself instead of reading it from a register. In the RV32I instructions considered here, `addi`, `andi`, `ori`, and `xori`, the immediate is extended to the register width before the operation. A negative immediate is extended by sign extension so that its negative value is preserved.
entries.example: `addi t1, t0, 4` adds the constant 4 specified in the instruction to the value in `t0`.
pitfalls: An immediate is an instruction operand, not an additional register.
For negative immediates, the higher-order bits must be set correctly by sign extension.
entries.heading: Immediate-Befehle: eigene kleine Beispiele

entries.term: Immediate instructions and sign extension (Immediate-Befehle und Sign Extension)
entries.short: In immediate instructions, the encoded constant is extended to the register width, with sign extension preserving the sign of negative values.
entries.explanation: In the RV32I immediate operations considered here, a negative immediate is extended to 32 bits by copying its sign bit. This preserves its signed numerical value instead of interpreting it as a small positive value. When a byte is loaded with `lb`, the sign of the loaded byte is also extended to the register width.
entries.example: A 12-bit immediate with the value −1 is extended to 32 bits as all ones and still represents −1.
pitfalls: Sign extension copies the sign bit; it does not always fill with zeros.
With `lb`, the loaded byte is sign-extended; other load instructions may use a different extension.
related: Bitwise logical instructions and immediate variants
entries.heading: Immediate-Befehle: eigene kleine Beispiele

entries.term: Bitwise logical instructions and immediate variants (Bitweise logische Befehle und Immediate-Varianten)
entries.short: `and`, `or`, and `xor` combine register bits bitwise, while their immediate variants `andi`, `ori`, and `xori` also use a constant from the instruction.
entries.explanation: `and` sets a result bit to 1 only when both input bits are 1; `or` sets it when at least one input bit is 1; `xor` sets it when the input bits differ. The variants `andi`, `ori`, and `xori` perform the same bitwise operations with an immediate. By contrast, `addi` adds the numerical value of the immediate and does not perform a bitwise logical operation. Sign extension must be taken into account for negative immediates.
entries.example: If `t0 = 0x2C`, `ori t2, t0, 0x10` yields `0x3C`, `xori t3, t0, 0x0F` yields `0x23`, and `andi t4, t0, 0x0F` yields `0x0C`.
pitfalls: XOR flips only bits at positions where one operand has a 1 and the other has a 0.
`andi` is a bitwise operation, not arithmetic subtraction.
entries.heading: Immediate-Befehle: eigene kleine Beispiele

entries.short: Checking registers, signs, and control flow step by step helps find common errors in assembly programming.
entries.explanation: Trace the code instruction by instruction and record the affected register values after each step. Note initial values, and assume zero only for `x0`. Before each arithmetic operation, determine whether the operands are intended as signed or unsigned and whether sign extension occurs. Plan the control flow and register allocation before writing, comment the code adequately, and for loops check the start, termination condition, and number of iterations. Observe the applicable register conventions for subroutine calls.
entries.example: Record the counter, termination test, and affected registers at each loop iteration to detect an execution that runs one iteration too many or too few.
pitfalls: Do not treat uninitialized register values as zero.
For signed byte values loaded with `lb`, account for sign extension.
Trace loop termination and register allocation instruction by instruction.
related: Signed and unsigned interpretation in M instructions
entries.heading: Typische Fehler beim Assemblerprogrammieren
